Each problem is shown //! in the part of the board it is played in, drawn in a symmetry of the board chosen at random. Undo takes back a //! move; once the problem is solved - by the book's line, the target's capture, or its group's life - "Solved" shows, //! and Next goes on to the next problem. There is no losing: a player who sees it will not come undoes and tries again. //! //! It is goban, made another way (`goban.appFor`): the rules, the problems (`goban.problem_sgfs`, made from //! published ones by goban_problems_tool.zig), the computer, the board and its sounds are all goban's. Only the choice //! of problems and of the two buttons are this file's. const goban = @import("goban"); /// goban's panic handler, which reports through the engine. pub const panic = goban.panic; /// What makes this app of goban's: its problems, one after another, and their two buttons. const variant: goban.AppVariant = .{ .title = "zimr - goban problems", .interface = .problem_buttons, .problems = &goban.alternating_problem_sgfs, }; /// The program. pub const app = goban.appFor(variant);

The build compiles this file into the kernel wasm the page's workers run (`kernel_deps` gives it goban's //! kernels.zig as `k_goban`); the program itself submits its jobs through goban's registry. const goban_kernels = @import("k_goban"); /// goban's kernels, by name. pub const job_kernels = goban_kernels.job_kernels; /// goban's registry. pub const registry = goban_kernels.registry;

//! goban - a Go board for two players on one screen. //! //! THE GAME //! Two players take turns placing stones, black first, on the intersections ("points") of a square grid. Stones of //! one colour that touch along the lines form a GROUP. The empty points next to a group are its LIBERTIES. A group //! left with no liberty is captured: its stones leave the board and become the capturer's PRISONERS. A move that //! would leave its own group with no liberty (SUICIDE) is refused, unless it captures first. A move may not retake a //! single stone at once in the back-and-forth called KO, which would otherwise repeat forever. //! In ATARI GO, a game for learning, the first player to capture a set number of stones wins. //! //! THE FOREST //! The program keeps every group as a tree whose nodes are the group's stones, the whole board being a forest of such //! trees (a disjoint-set forest, or union-find). Every stone points to a PARENT; following parents ends at the ROOT, //! the stone that stands for its group and holds the group's liberties and stone list. Two stones are in one group //! exactly when they reach the same root. //! //! stones on the board parent pointers what the root holds //! //! . X X . . > v . root (2,2): //! . . X . . . v . stones (0,1) (0,2) (1,2) (2,2) //! . . X . . . R . liberties (0,0) (0,3) (1,1) (1,3) ... //! //! (> and v point right and down to a stone's parent; R is the root, (2,2), its own parent) //! //! Placing a stone joins it to the groups it touches: their roots get the new stone as their parent, so the newest //! stone becomes the root of the whole joined group, and the joined groups' liberties and stones move into its sets. //! Finding a root later shortens the path it walks ("path compression"), so the trees stay flat. A move therefore //! costs a few set operations, where a search of the whole group (a "flood fill") would visit every stone. //! //! THE SECTIONS (each opens with a `// ===== N. Name =====` banner and a lesson of its own) //! 1. Stones and points a point's index, its row and column, its neighbours //! 2. The forest Position: the stones, the parents, each root's liberties and stones //! 3. The rules which moves are legal, and what a move does: joins, captures, ko, the turn //! 4. The record the setup and the moves; starting a game; undo and redo by replay //! 5. Checking the forest a flood fill from the stones alone, compared with every root's sets //! 6. Diagrams a position as text, written and read, for tests and the clipboard //! 7. The opponent Monte Carlo tree search for Atari Go: the tree, its iterations, the move chosen //! 8. Layout the board's place in the window, and from a pointer to a point //! 9. Drawing the wood, the lines, the star points, the stones, the last move, the ghost //! 10. Input press, drag, release: picking a stone up and putting it down //! 11. The app the state, the buttons and the pause window, and one frame //! const z = @import("zimr"); const common = @import("example_common"); const ui = z.ui_real; const jobs = z.jobs; const builtin = @import("builtin"); const Allocator = std.mem.Allocator; const ArenaAllocator = std.heap.ArenaAllocator; const sortSlice = std.mem.sort; const readInt = std.mem.readInt; const writeInt = std.mem.writeInt; // ===== 1. Stones and points ===== // // The board is a square of `board_size` x `board_size` points, from 3 x 3 up to 19 x 19. A point is named by one // number, its index in reading order: row 0 holds points 0 .. board_size - 1, row 1 the next board_size, and so on. // // col: 0 1 2 on a 3 x 3 board: pointAt(1, 2) = 1 * 3 + 2 = 5 // row 0 0 - 1 - 2 rowOf(5) = 5 / 3 = 1 // row 1 3 - 4 - 5 colOf(5) = 5 % 3 = 2 // row 2 6 - 7 - 8 // // One number per point lets every per-point table be a plain array indexed by point, and a set of points be a bit // set. Every table is sized for the largest board, so changing the board size allocates nothing; a smaller board uses // the first board_size * board_size entries. // // These functions take the board size as an argument rather than reading it from somewhere: the size is part of the // position (section 2), and nothing in this file is global. /// The sizes a board may have. They are compile-time constants, because the largest board sizes every per-point /// table, and they live in this namespace so that every use names what it is a limit of: `board_limits.max_size`. pub const board_limits = struct { /// The smallest board: a 3 x 3 board still has a centre point and four corners. pub const min_size: u8 = 3; /// The largest board, the standard one. pub const max_size: u8 = 19; /// Points on the largest board, 19 x 19 = 361: the length of every per-point table. pub const max_points: usize = @as(usize, max_size) * max_size; /// The most neighbours a point can have: up, down, left and right. The length of the buffer neighborsOf fills. pub const max_neighbors: usize = 4; /// The most star points a board has: four corners, four sides and the centre (section 9). pub const max_star_points: usize = 9; }; /// A point of the board, as its index in reading order: `row * board_size + col`. /// An absent point - no ko point, no last move - is `null` in a `?Point`. pub const Point = u16; /// A set of points: one bit per point of the largest board. Adding, removing and testing a point are one bit /// operation each, the union of two sets is one OR per machine word, and nothing is ever allocated. pub const PointSet = StaticBitSet(board_limits.max_points); /// What stands on a point: nothing, a black stone or a white stone. The same type names a player - the player whose /// stones are that colour - so `player_to_move` and `winner` are Stones too. pub const Stone = enum(u8) { none, black, white, /// The other player. Asking for the opponent of `.none` is a bug in the caller, so it asserts. pub fn opponent(stone: Stone) Stone { assertf(stone != .none, @src(), "opponent() asked for the opponent of an empty point", .{}); switch (stone) { .black => { return .white; }, .white => { return .black; }, .none => { unreachable; }, } } }; /// How many points a board of this size has: board_size * board_size. pub fn pointCount(board_size: u8) usize { assertf( board_size >= board_limits.min_size and board_size <= board_limits.max_size, @src(), "board size {d} is outside {d}..{d}", .{ board_size, board_limits.min_size, board_limits.max_size }, ); const side: usize = board_size; const point_count: usize = side * side; return point_count; } /// Is (row, col) a point of the board? Rows and columns are signed here, because the questions this answers come from /// arithmetic that can step off the board on either side: a neighbour's row - 1, or a pointer left of the board. pub fn isOnBoard(board_size: u8, row: i32, col: i32) bool { const row_is_on_board: bool = row >= 0 and row < board_size; const col_is_on_board: bool = col >= 0 and col < board_size; const point_is_on_board: bool = row_is_on_board and col_is_on_board; return point_is_on_board; } /// The point at (row, col): its index in reading order, `row * board_size + col`. pub fn pointAt(board_size: u8, row: u8, col: u8) Point { assertf( isOnBoard(board_size, row, col), @src(), "pointAt({d}, {d}) is off a {d} x {d} board", .{ row, col, board_size, board_size }, ); const side: Point = board_size; const rows_above: Point = row; const point: Point = rows_above * side + col; return point; } /// The row of a point: how many whole rows come before it in reading order. pub fn rowOf(board_size: u8, point: Point) u8 { assertf(point < pointCount(board_size), @src(), "point {d} is off a {d} x {d} board", .{ point, board_size, board_size, }); const side: Point = board_size; const row: u8 = @intCast(point / side); return row; } /// The column of a point: how far along its row it is. pub fn colOf(board_size: u8, point: Point) u8 { assertf(point < pointCount(board_size), @src(), "point {d} is off a {d} x {d} board", .{ point, board_size, board_size, }); const side: Point = board_size; const col: u8 = @intCast(point % side); return col; } /// The neighbours of `point`: the points one line away, up, down, left and right, in that order, leaving out the /// ones that would be off the board. A point in the middle has four, a point on an edge three, a corner two. /// They are written into the caller's buffer, and the returned slice is the part of it that holds them; it is valid /// for as long as the buffer is. Every append fits, since no point has more than `board_limits.max_neighbors`. pub fn neighborsOf( board_size: u8, point: Point, out_buffer: *[board_limits.max_neighbors]Point, ) []const Point { const row: u8 = rowOf(board_size, point); const col: u8 = colOf(board_size, point); const last_line: u8 = board_size - 1; var neighbors: ArrayList(Point) = .initBuffer(out_buffer); const has_point_above: bool = row > 0; if (has_point_above) { neighbors.appendAssumeCapacity(pointAt(board_size, row - 1, col)); } const has_point_below: bool = row < last_line; if (has_point_below) { neighbors.appendAssumeCapacity(pointAt(board_size, row + 1, col)); } const has_point_left: bool = col > 0; if (has_point_left) { neighbors.appendAssumeCapacity(pointAt(board_size, row, col - 1)); } const has_point_right: bool = col < last_line; if (has_point_right) { neighbors.appendAssumeCapacity(pointAt(board_size, row, col + 1)); } return neighbors.items; } /// A rectangle of the board's points, its first and last row and column included: the region a problem is /// played in (section 3's lesson). Moves outside it are not moves of the problem. pub const ProblemRegion = struct { first_row: u8, first_col: u8, last_row: u8, last_col: u8, /// Whether `point` of a board this size is in the region. pub fn contains(region: ProblemRegion, board_size: u8, point: Point) bool { const row: u8 = rowOf(board_size, point); const col: u8 = colOf(board_size, point); const row_is_inside: bool = row >= region.first_row and row <= region.last_row; const col_is_inside: bool = col >= region.first_col and col <= region.last_col; return row_is_inside and col_is_inside; } /// The smallest rectangle around `points` widened by `margin` lines on every side, within a board this size. /// `points` must not be empty. pub fn around(board_size: u8, points: []const Point, margin: u8) ProblemRegion { assertf(points.len > 0, @src(), "ProblemRegion.around: no points", .{}); var region: ProblemRegion = .{ .first_row = maxInt(u8), .first_col = maxInt(u8), .last_row = 0, .last_col = 0 }; for (points) |point| { region.first_row = @min(region.first_row, rowOf(board_size, point)); region.first_col = @min(region.first_col, colOf(board_size, point)); region.last_row = @max(region.last_row, rowOf(board_size, point)); region.last_col = @max(region.last_col, colOf(board_size, point)); } const last_line: u8 = board_size - 1; region.first_row -|= margin; region.first_col -|= margin; region.last_row = @min(region.last_row + margin, last_line); region.last_col = @min(region.last_col + margin, last_line); return region; } }; // ===== 2. The forest ===== // // A Position is what is on the board now: the stones, and the forest that groups them (the header draws it). Every // table has one entry per point; the group tables are read only at a group's root. // // group_parent[p] the stone p points to. A root points to itself; an empty point has no parent (null). // group_liberties[r] for a root r: the empty points next to any stone of r's group. // group_stones[r] for a root r: every stone of r's group, r included. // // Away from the roots, group_liberties and group_stones are empty: a stone is a root when it is placed, and its sets // are emptied when its group joins another or is captured. The functions below keep that true, and read the sets // only at a root. // // Three operations change the forest, and all three are used only while a stone is being placed (section 3): // // findRootCompressingPath find a stone's root, and make every stone passed on the way a child of the root // joinGroups hang one group's tree under another's root, and move its sets there // removeCapturedGroup take a captured group off the board, and give its points back as liberties // // Everything that only looks at the board - the suicide test, the overlays, the inspector - uses findRoot, which // follows the same parents and changes nothing. So the shape of the forest follows from the moves played alone, and // replaying a game rebuilds the same forest. If every search compressed paths, the forest's shape would depend on // every question ever asked of it - drawing the board included - and a drawing of the forest would show where the // mouse had been as much as what the moves made. /// What is on the board now, and everything the rules need to know about it. How the game got here - the moves - /// is not part of it. pub const Position = struct { /// Points per side, board_limits.min_size .. board_limits.max_size. board_size: u8, /// What stands on each point. stones: [board_limits.max_points]Stone, /// The forest: each stone's parent in its group's tree, itself at a root, null on an empty point. group_parent: [board_limits.max_points]?Point, /// Meaningful at a root only: the group's liberties. group_liberties: [board_limits.max_points]PointSet, /// Meaningful at a root only: the group's stones. group_stones: [board_limits.max_points]PointSet, /// The point the player to move may not play this turn because of ko, if any. ko_point: ?Point, /// Whose turn it is. player_to_move: Stone, /// The stone placed by the last move, for its marker; null before the first move. last_move: ?Point, /// White stones captured by black so far: black's prisoners. stones_captured_by_black: u32, /// Black stones captured by white so far: white's prisoners. stones_captured_by_white: u32, /// Atari Go: the first player to capture this many stones wins. Null in plain Go. capture_goal: ?u8, /// A problem's target (section 3's lesson): the stone whose capture wins the game for its opponent - in a kill /// problem a white stone black must capture, in a life problem a black stone white must not. Null in a game. target: ?Point, /// A problem: the region its moves are played in. Null in a game, whose moves may go anywhere. region: ?ProblemRegion, /// The player who reached the capture goal, or captured the target, once one has. winner: ?Stone, /// An empty board of `board_size`, black to play, no captures, plain Go. pub fn init(board_size: u8) Position { assertf( board_size >= board_limits.min_size and board_size <= board_limits.max_size, @src(), "board size {d} is outside {d}..{d}", .{ board_size, board_limits.min_size, board_limits.max_size }, ); const empty_board: Position = .{ .board_size = board_size, .stones = @splat(.none), .group_parent = @splat(null), .group_liberties = @splat(.empty), .group_stones = @splat(.empty), .ko_point = null, .player_to_move = .black, .last_move = null, .stones_captured_by_black = 0, .stones_captured_by_white = 0, .capture_goal = null, .target = null, .region = null, .winner = null, }; return empty_board; } }; /// Does `point` hold a stone that is its own parent - the root of its group? pub fn isRoot(position: *const Position, point: Point) bool { const maybe_parent: ?Point = position.group_parent[point]; const has_parent: bool = maybe_parent != null; if (!has_parent) { return false; } const parent: Point = maybe_parent.?; const is_own_parent: bool = parent == point; return is_own_parent; } /// The parent of the stone on `point`. Every stone has one - a root is its own - so a stone without a parent means the /// forest is broken, and this asserts. fn parentOf(position: *const Position, point: Point) Point { const maybe_parent: ?Point = position.group_parent[point]; assertf(maybe_parent != null, @src(), "the stone on point {d} has no parent", .{point}); const parent: Point = maybe_parent.?; return parent; } /// The root of the group that the stone on `point` belongs to: follow parents until a stone is its own parent. /// /// a -> b -> c -> root findRoot(a) = root, after three steps; the forest is left as it was /// /// Read-only, so everything that only looks at the board uses this one (the section's lesson says why that matters). /// Each step goes one stone closer to the root, so a walk longer than the board has points has found a loop of /// parents, and asserts. pub fn findRoot(position: *const Position, point: Point) Point { assertf(position.stones[point] != .none, @src(), "findRoot asked about empty point {d}", .{point}); var current: Point = point; var steps_taken: usize = 0; while (true) { const parent: Point = parentOf(position, current); const current_is_root: bool = parent == current; if (current_is_root) { return current; } steps_taken += 1; assertf( steps_taken < board_limits.max_points, @src(), "the parents from point {d} loop without reaching a root", .{point}, ); current = parent; } } /// The root of `point`'s group, as findRoot finds it, and on the way every stone of the path is made a child of the /// root ("path compression"), so the next search from any of them takes one step. /// /// before: a -> b -> c -> root after: a -> root /// b -> root /// c -> root (c's parent was already the root) /// /// Two passes: findRoot walks to the root, then the same path is walked again, each stone repointed at the root as it /// is left. It changes the forest, so it is used only while a stone is being placed. pub fn findRootCompressingPath(position: *Position, point: Point) Point { const root: Point = findRoot(position, point); var current: Point = point; while (current != root) { const next_on_path: Point = parentOf(position, current); position.group_parent[current] = root; current = next_on_path; } return root; } /// Joins two groups of one colour into one, rooted at `new_root`: the joining group's root takes `new_root` as its /// parent, so its whole tree hangs under `new_root`, and its liberties and stones move into `new_root`'s sets. /// /// new_root's group: N joining group: J <- s after: N <- J <- s /// /// The rules call it with the stone just placed as `new_root`, so the newest stone becomes the root of every group /// it touches. Returns whether two groups were joined: false when both roots are already the same group's - a placed /// stone can touch one group on two sides, and the second side finds the group already joined. pub fn joinGroups(position: *Position, new_root: Point, joining_root: Point) bool { const already_one_group: bool = new_root == joining_root; if (already_one_group) { return false; } assertf(isRoot(position, new_root), @src(), "joinGroups: new_root {d} is not a root", .{new_root}); assertf(isRoot(position, joining_root), @src(), "joinGroups: joining_root {d} is not a root", .{joining_root}); const new_root_stone: Stone = position.stones[new_root]; const joining_root_stone: Stone = position.stones[joining_root]; assertf(new_root_stone == joining_root_stone, @src(), "joinGroups: {d} is {t} and {d} is {t}", .{ new_root, new_root_stone, joining_root, joining_root_stone, }); position.group_parent[joining_root] = new_root; const joining_liberties: PointSet = position.group_liberties[joining_root]; const joining_stones: PointSet = position.group_stones[joining_root]; position.group_liberties[new_root].setUnion(joining_liberties); position.group_stones[new_root].setUnion(joining_stones); position.group_liberties[joining_root] = .empty; position.group_stones[joining_root] = .empty; return true; } /// Takes a captured group off the board and returns the points it emptied. /// The group must have no liberty left: that is what captured means. /// /// before: . O . O's root has no liberty after: . O . /// O X O X is captured O . O the emptied point is now a /// . O . . O . liberty of all four O groups /// /// First every stone of the group leaves the board. Then each emptied point is given, as a liberty, to every group of /// the capturing colour beside it: the stones that did the capturing get that breathing space back. Points beside an /// emptied point that were also in the captured group are empty by then, and get nothing. pub fn removeCapturedGroup(position: *Position, captured_root: Point) PointSet { assertf(isRoot(position, captured_root), @src(), "removeCapturedGroup: {d} is not a root", .{captured_root}); const liberty_count: usize = position.group_liberties[captured_root].count(); assertf(liberty_count == 0, @src(), "removeCapturedGroup: group {d} still has {d} liberties", .{ captured_root, liberty_count, }); const captured_stone: Stone = position.stones[captured_root]; const capturing_stone: Stone = captured_stone.opponent(); const captured_points: PointSet = position.group_stones[captured_root]; // Empty every point of the group. The root's sets go with it; the others were emptied when their groups joined. var points_to_empty: PointSet.Iterator(.{}) = captured_points.iterator(.{}); while (points_to_empty.next()) |point_index| { const emptied_point: Point = @intCast(point_index); position.stones[emptied_point] = .none; position.group_parent[emptied_point] = null; } position.group_stones[captured_root] = .empty; // Give each emptied point to the capturing groups beside it. var points_to_give: PointSet.Iterator(.{}) = captured_points.iterator(.{}); while (points_to_give.next()) |point_index| { const emptied_point: Point = @intCast(point_index); var neighbor_buffer: [board_limits.max_neighbors]Point = undefined; const neighbors: []const Point = neighborsOf(position.board_size, emptied_point, &neighbor_buffer); for (neighbors) |neighbor| { const neighbor_is_capturer: bool = position.stones[neighbor] == capturing_stone; if (neighbor_is_capturer) { const capturer_root: Point = findRootCompressingPath(position, neighbor); position.group_liberties[capturer_root].set(emptied_point); } } } return captured_points; } // ===== 3. The rules ===== // // A move is one stone placed by the player to move. Whether it may be played is decided by checkMove, from four // conditions; what it does to the board is placeStone, which follows the rules in the order they apply: // // 1. the stone stands on the point, a group of one; // 2. its empty neighbours are its liberties, and every group beside it loses this point as a liberty; // 3. it joins the groups of its own colour beside it, into one group with the new stone as root; // 4. every enemy group beside it that has no liberty left is captured; // 5. the ko point is set if the move took exactly one stone back and forth (below); // 6. the prisoners are counted, an Atari Go win is noted, and the turn passes. // // Captures come before the suicide question. A stone that fills an enemy group's last liberty captures it, and the // emptied points become its own liberties, so a move that looks like suicide is legal when it captures. That is why // wouldBeSuicide counts an enemy neighbour with one liberty as a way out. // // KO. Black captures one white stone by playing into the point it was attacking from; if White could at once play // back on the emptied point, capturing Black's stone, the two could repeat forever: // // . X O . . X O . . X O . // X O . O Black X . X O White X O . O the same position again // . X O . plays . X O . retakes . X O . // // So the point of a single captured stone is forbidden for one turn - but only when the capture has that shape: the // capturing stone stands alone, and its one liberty is the point it just emptied, so a retake there would capture it // in turn. Any other capture of one stone leaves the point open. In a SNAPBACK, the stone that captures one joins a // group of its own colour that is left with that point as its one liberty; the opponent may play there at once and // capture the whole group, which is legal Go. A ko rule that forbade the point after every capture of one stone // would refuse snapbacks. // // PROBLEMS. A go problem is played as a capture: one stone is its TARGET, and capturing it wins for its opponent - in // a kill problem black captures a white target, in a life problem white must not capture a black one. Its moves are // played in its REGION, the box around its stones and one line beyond; a move outside it is refused like an illegal // one, so a player's input and the computer's search both stay inside. // // UNCONDITIONAL LIFE (Benson's algorithm, 1976). A group is alive unconditionally when the opponent cannot capture it // however he plays, even if its owner never moves again. Take the board's chains of one colour, and its regions - the // connected sets of points with no stone of that colour. A region is VITAL to a chain beside it when every empty point // of it is that chain's liberty: the opponent could only fill it by playing on the chain's liberties, and a chain // with two such regions keeps one empty to the end. So, until nothing changes, every chain with fewer than two vital // regions is set aside, and every region beside a chain set aside goes with it - a region bounded partly by a chain // that may die is no safe eye for the rest. What is left is alive: // // . X . X O two eyes, (0, 0) and (0, 2): each a region of one empty point that is black's // X X X X O liberty, so both vital - alive. So the forest gets an independent check: recompute every group from the stones alone, and compare. // // The recomputation is a FLOOD FILL, the simplest way to find a group. } /// One parent pointer of the forest: a stone, and the stone it points to. pub const ForestArrow = struct { from: Point, to: Point, }; /// Every parent pointer of the forest - one per stone that is not a root, so a group of n stones has n - 1 - written /// into the caller's buffer in reading order: what the forest view draws. pub fn forestArrows( position: *const Position, out_buffer: *[board_limits.max_points]ForestArrow, ) []const ForestArrow { var arrows: ArrayList(ForestArrow) = .initBuffer(out_buffer); Diagrams ===== // // A position can be written as text, one line per row of the board, the way Go books print a position: // // // goban 5x5, white to play // . . X O . // X O O . . // . . . . . // . . . . . // . . . . . // // `X` is a black stone, `O` a white stone, `.` an empty point; spaces between them are optional. The first line, if // it starts with `//`, says whose turn it is; without it, black is to play. The number of rows is the board size, // from board_limits.min_size to board_limits.max_size, and every row is that long. // // Reading a diagram is the way a position gets into the program without its moves: from a test, or pasted from the // clipboard. A diagram carries the stones and the turn and nothing else - no moves, no ko point, no prisoners - so // it starts a game whose record holds the stones as its setup (section 4), and undo stops there. A diagram that does // not describe a position is refused, with what is wrong and where: a row of the wrong length, a character that is // not a stone, or a group with no liberty, which no game can reach because it would have been captured. // // SGF, the Smart Game Format, is how go programs and problem collections write games. A file is a tree of nodes in // parentheses, each node a `;` and its properties, each property an identifier and one or more values in brackets: // // (;SZ[19]AB[op][pp]AW[pq][qq]TR[qq]C[Black to play.] // (;B[rs];W[rr];B[ns]C[Correct]) // (;B[rq];W[rr])) // // A point is two letters, its column and then its row, `a` the first from the left and from the top: `pq` is column // 15, row 16. The root node - the first - sets the problem up: `SZ` the board size, `AB` and `AW` the black and white // stones (a value `aa:cc` is the whole rectangle between two points), and the branches after it are the solution's // variations. A KILL PROBLEM is black to play and kill a white group, a LIFE PROBLEM black to play and make a black // group live; goban's problems carry one mark the published ones do not, on the problem's target - a triangle (`TR`) // on the white stone black must capture, or a square (`SQ`) on the black stone black must save. Reading one takes its // root node (the solution tree is read apart, `readSolutionTree`, the book the computer may follow) and refuses what // no position could be: a point off the board or given two stones, a group with no liberty, a root marking no stone // of the right colour, or more than one. /// The character that shows a stone in a diagram. pub fn diagramSymbol(stone: Stone) u8 { switch (stone) { .none => { return '.'; }, .black => { return 'X'; }, .white => { return 'O'; }, } } /// The stone a diagram's character shows, or null when the character is not one of `.`, `X` and `O`. pub fn stoneOfSymbol(character: u8) ?Stone { switch (character) { '.' => { return .none; separator = ", "; } if (report.captured_count > 0) { try writer.print("{s}captured {d}", .{ separator, report.captured_count }); separator = ", "; } if (report.ko_point) |ko_point| { const ko_row: u8 = rowOf(board_size, ko_point); // ===== 7. The opponent ===== // // The computer plays Atari Go by MONTE CARLO TREE SEARCH (MCTS). A program that plays a board game must know how good // a position is, and plain Go makes that hard: who is ahead depends on territory settled only at the end of a long // game. Atari Go removes the difficulty - the game ends the moment a player reaches the capture goal, often within a // few dozen moves on a 9 x 9 board - so a game played out at random from any position reaches a real result, a win or // a loss, with no judgement of the board at all. MCTS is built on exactly that: it plays many such games, PLAYOUTS, // and keeps the statistics of their first moves in a tree that grows toward the moves that win. // // Each node of the tree is a position, reached from its parent's by one move; it counts the playouts that went // through it (its VISITS) and how many of them the player who made its move went on to win. One ITERATION of the // search adds one node and one playout, in four steps (the UCT form of Kocsis and Szepesvari, 2006): // // 1. selection from the root, go down the tree: at each node whose moves all have children, to the child // with the highest upper confidence bound (UCB1, below) // 2. expansion at the first node with a legal move that has no child yet, add that move's child // 3. simulation from the new child's position, play random legal moves until a player reaches the goal // 4. backpropagation from the new child back to the root, every node counts one visit more, and a win more when // the player who made its move is the playout's winner // // UCB1 weighs what a move has won against how little it has been tried: // // bound(child) = wins / visits + c * sqrt( ln(parent's visits) / visits ) // // = wins / visits + c * sqrt(ln(parent's visits)) / sqrt(visits) // '-------- the same for every child of one parent: worked out once // // The first term favours the moves that have won; the second grows for a move left untried while its siblings are // played, so every move is tried again from time to time and none is written off on a few unlucky playouts. The // constant c sets the balance. sqrt(2) is the value for which UCB1's guarantee is proven when results are 0 or 1; but // that guarantee is about trying every move enough in the long run, and a search of a few thousand iterations does // better to deepen its best moves sooner - this one uses 0.6, which plays Atari Go stronger. // A node's wins are counted for the player who made its move - the player choosing among it and its siblings at // the parent - so at every level the bound measures the move from the point of view of the player who would make it. // // After the iterations, the move played is the root's most visited child - or, when the root has one candidate only (a // capture that wins, the only legal move), that move at once, with no time spent on a choice there is not. Visits are // the steadier measure: a win rate can be inflated by a few lucky playouts, but the search sends its visits to the // move whose wins hold up. // // 2000 iterations, black to play, a goal of one capture: // // . . a . . the root's children, most visited first: // . X O X . a (0, 2) 148 visits, 296 of 296 half-wins - it captures, and wins at once // . . X . . (0, 3) 136 visits, 268 of 272 half-wins // . . . . . (0, 1) 136 visits, 268 of 272 half-wins // . . . . . ... 18 more // // Every playout through a is a win, so its win rate is 1 and it gets the most visits. The other moves are nearly as // good, and the search says so: the white stone cannot escape - extending to a leaves it one liberty, and black takes // it there - so after almost any move black still wins. The exploration term keeps giving them a share, and the // more iterations, the larger a's lead. // // THE TREE IS ONE ARRAY. Its nodes are `extern struct`s in one array, joined by indices rather than pointers: a node // names its parent, its first child and its next sibling. So the tree is one contiguous block of bytes, which can be // handed to a job and taken back whole, with nothing to fix up, and an `extern struct`'s layout is the same in every // compile. A node does not store its untried moves: a node's children are made in the order of its position's // candidate moves (`candidateMoves`, below; the legal moves among them are the rules' to say - ko, suicide and a game // already won are never the search's business), so a count of the children made says which candidate is next. A // node's candidates are counted the first time an iteration expands it, not when it is made: most nodes are made by // one iteration and never reached again, and counting them takes a pass over the board. Wins are counted in // HALF-WINS - 2 for a win, 1 for a playout that ended undecided - so every count is an integer. // // Each iteration starts from a copy of the root position - a Position is fixed arrays, so the copy is one memory // copy, and nothing is allocated - and plays the selected moves on it; the root position itself is only read. The // random generator the playouts draw from keeps its state in the tree, so a search continued later draws the same // numbers as one run without a pause: the same seed and the same count of iterations give the same tree. // // THE TREE IS KEPT BETWEEN MOVES. After the computer's move and the reply, the node of that pair of moves is the root // of a subtree the last search already explored, and its visits are a head start for the next one: // // root (the computer to play) the next search's root, copied out with // |- a the computer's move ............ everything under it: // | |- b the person's reply ........ ----> b' // | | |- ... |- ... // | '- ... // '- ... // // So a tree records which game it belongs to: how many of the record's moves had been played at its root, and a // fingerprint of the root's position. A later search replays the record to that point and compares fingerprints; // if they agree, it follows the moves played since through the tree's children, and the node it reaches becomes // the root of a fresh array holding its subtree (`takeUpSubtree`). A tree that does not lead there - a new game, an // undo, a pasted position, a reply the search never tried - is not taken up, and the search starts afresh. // `continueSearch` does all of it, given the record and the last tree. When no move has been played since the last // tree's root - a search cut into slices, one after another - the tree is the search's own, and goes on in place; // since its generator's state goes on with it, the slices make the very tree one search of all their iterations // would have made. // // A tree goes to a job and comes back as bytes: its header, then its nodes (`writeTree`, `readTree`). Both are // `extern struct`s, so their bytes mean the same to the program and to the job's separate compile. // // THE SEARCH AS A JOB. A search of a second would hold up the program's frames for a second, so it runs as a job of // zimr's job system (`z.jobs`): a pure function, run on a worker of its own - a Web Worker in a page, a thread in a // native program - while the board keeps drawing. A job is given a small header and a payload of bytes, and writes // its result as bytes; it keeps nothing from one job to the next. So everything the search needs travels with it: // // header SearchJobHeader: the settings, the count of iterations, the seed of a fresh tree // payload the record - the board, the goal, the setup stones, the moves played - then the last tree's bytes, // or nothing when there is none // result the tree after the iterations, as bytes // // The job runs in a separate compile, whose plain structs need not be laid out as the program's are, so every byte // that crosses is an `extern struct`'s or a plain number's, and the record is written field by field rather than // copied whole (`writeSearchPayload`, `readSearchPayload`). The job itself is `searchJob`, listed in `kernels.zig`. // // DECISIVE MOVES. A node's candidate moves are its legal moves - unless its player can win at once, by a capture that // brings their prisoners to the goal: then the winning moves are its only candidates (Teytaud and Teytaud, 2010). The // search must otherwise make every child of a node before it chooses among them, and a reply that wins is only as // early among them as its point is on the board. Here white must escape at a, and every other move loses: // // . . . . . . . . . // . . . . . . . . . black's last move left white's stone at (3, 4) one liberty, a. Under each of white's // . . . . X . . . . 76 moves but a, black's winning capture at a is a reply among 75, about the 33rd // . . . X O a . . . made; until it is, black's replies are moves at random, and the losing move looks // . . . O X . . . . sound - on 5,000 iterations, white chose (4, 5), and lost. With decisive moves, // . . . . . . . . . black's one candidate under each such move is the capture: it wins every playout, // . . . . . . . . . and a few visits bring the move's win rate to nothing. Then the visits go to a. // // A PLAYOUT plays moves until a player reaches the goal. A LIGHT playout draws every move uniformly at random from the // legal moves. A HEAVY one first plays the URGENT MOVE, the two that matter most in Atari Go: // // capture: a group of the opponent's is in atari rescue: a group of one's own is in atari // // . . . . . . . . . . // . . X . . white's stone has one liberty, . . O . . black's stone has one liberty, at a: // . X O X . at a: black captures it there . O X a . black extends there // . . a . . (with a goal of one, that wins) . . O . . // . . . . . . . . . . // // A capture comes before a rescue, and among several of a kind one is drawn at random. When neither applies, the move // is a random legal move. Random play misses both: it leaves a capturable group standing, or lets its own be taken, // about as often as not, so a light playout's result says little about the position it started from. Playing the // urgent moves makes the playouts play the way the game is decided, and each playout tells the search more. // // The urgent moves are looked for over the whole board, not only around the last move. A group can stay in atari // across several moves - its owner played elsewhere - and a playout that looked only at the last move would leave it // standing; the search would then judge leaving a group in atari to be nearly safe, which in Atari Go is the one // thing it is not. The look costs one pass over the board's roots, the same order as the listing of empty points a // random move makes. // // A playout that finds no legal move, or is still undecided after `playout_move_cap` moves, counts as half a win for // each side. /// How a playout chooses its moves (the section's lesson). A byte, as it travels in a job's header. pub const PlayoutKind = enum(u8) { /// Every move drawn uniformly at random from the legal moves. light, /// The urgent move first - capture an opponent's group in atari, else rescue one of one's own - and a random /// legal move when there is none. heavy, }; /// How a search's move is chosen from the root's children (the section's lesson). A byte, as it travels in a job's /// header. pub const MoveChoice = enum(u8) { /// The most visited child: the visits go to the move whose wins hold up. most_visited, /// The child whose win rate is most surely high (KataGo's lower confidence bound): its win rate less /// `confidence_stdevs` standard errors, among the children with at least `confidence_min_share` of the most /// visited child's visits. A pointer over one of them is over no // point of the board, so a press on a button never picks up a stone, and a stone carried onto a button and let go // there is put back. While // either window is open the board below is dimmed and its two buttons are disabled, so nothing behind a window // can be pressed by mistake. The mouse's side button takes back a move, as Undo does. The interface is zimr's port of // Dear ImGui; its sizes are measured in its font size, which follows the window's width and height // (`interfaceFontSize`), so the buttons stay finger-sized on a phone, do not grow past a comfortable size on a desktop, // and the tallest window, measured as it is shown, still fits a phone held sideways. The pause window's "Sound" // switch turns them off. A page may sound only after the person's first press, which it waits for anywhere on the // page: in goban that press is always the main menu's, so by the first stone the sound is running, and goban needs // no start screen of its own. // // A game frame runs in this order: // // begin the frame and the interface; submit the windows the interface now knows where its windows are // carry out what the buttons asked Undo, Menu, the pause window's choices // read the board's input, unless the interface has it press, drag, release (section 10) // move the ghost; draw the wood, the board and the ghost // draw the interface on top; end the frame // // The windows are submitted before the board's input is read, because only then can the interface say whether the // pointer is over one of them; the interface is drawn last, so it is never hidden under the board. // // THE COMPUTER'S TURN. On the // computer's turn the board takes no stone and the caption says it is thinking, while its search (section 7) runs as // a job, frame after frame, until the move's iterations are done: // // its turn, no job running -> a job: the record and the last tree go to it // a job running -> polled; nothing yet // the job's tree landed -> kept, to go with the next job; if the move's iterations are all run, its // most visited move is played as a person's would be // // A move's search runs for a second of the monotonic clock, as many iterations as the machine runs in that time. // Where there is a worker or a thread, the second is a run of jobs (`JobSearch`), each sized from the rate the last // one ran at to take about a tenth of it, each taking up the tree the last returned; a job, in a kernel that imports // nothing, has no clock of its own, so the program keeps the time. The build requires this file of an app with jobs, and compiles it into the separate kernel wasm the workers run, //! which must import nothing. The search, and its registry, are in `goban.zig`, section 7 (`searchJob`, //! `search_job_registry`): this file only lists them.
